severities.error: Stops compilation, or stops the bar. Nothing is drawn from a bar that raised one.
severities.warning: Never stops anything. Reported on the line and in the editor's gutter.

stages.check: Names, types, scope and call sites, before any bar runs.
stages.host: The host answering the engine: data, limits and order destinations.
stages.import: Reading a script written in another chart language and writing it as OpenScript.

ranges.means: The source text is not a program: characters, layout and grammar.
The program parses, and a name or a type does not work out.
A call or an option is wrong at the call site.
A bar produced a value the engine cannot act on.
A budget was exhausted: loops, memory, size or time.
Bars, instruments, timeframes and the host's answers to requests.
An order could not be placed as written.
The script compiles and runs, and something in it is probably not meant.
A script written in another chart language could not be translated as written, or was translated with a stated difference.

entries.title: Unexpected character
entries.message: Unexpected character {char}. {suggestion}

placeholders.char: the offending character, quoted, with its Unicode name when it is not an ASCII graphic
placeholders.suggestion: the replacement sentence for this character, from the substitution table in section 7 of this document

entries.cause: Outside a string literal the language accepts ASCII letters, ASCII digits, space, newline and the punctuation list of language.md 3.12, and nothing else. A non-breaking space pasted from a web page, a typographic quotation mark pasted from a word processor, a non-ASCII letter in a name, and an operator the language does not have (!, &&, ||, ^, {, }) all arrive here. The character is rejected where it sits rather than three tokens later, because an invisible character produces a baffling parse error otherwise. Two runs whose every character is legal are not this code: a name written against a number is OS1029, and a colour literal with the wrong number of digits is OS1027. Naming one character of either and advising its deletion, which is what this fix says to do, would leave a program that still compiles and means something else.
entries.fix: Delete the character or replace it with the plain ASCII spelling the message names: a plain space for a non-breaking space, a straight quote for a typographic one, not for !, and for &&, or for ||, pow(a, b) for ^.

entries.title: Tab in indentation
entries.message: This line is indented with a tab.
entries.cause: Leading whitespace is spaces only. A tab is rejected rather than expanded because the width of a tab is an editor setting, so a file whose block structure depends on it means something different when someone else opens it.
entries.fix: Replace the leading tabs with spaces. Four spaces per level is the convention and the formatter's output.

entries.title: Indentation does not match this block
entries.message: This line is indented {found} spaces; the block opened at line {line} is indented {expected}.

placeholders.found: the leading space count on this line
placeholders.expected: the leading space count every line of this block carries
placeholders.line: the line that opened the block

entries.cause: Every line of one block carries exactly the same leading whitespace. A difference of one space is still a difference, because the alternative is a language where a block's extent depends on a tolerance nobody can see. A blank line and a comment-only line stand outside the rule: they carry no token and no indentation at all, so any leading whitespace is accepted on them and neither one is ever this error. A continuation line stands outside it for a different reason: it belongs to a statement that began above it and opens no block, so what its indentation has to clear is that statement rather than a block, and that is OS1028.
entries.fix: Indent this line to {expected} spaces to keep it in the block, or to {line}'s own indentation to end the block here.

example.before:
if trending
    body = close - open
     wick = high - low
example.after:
if trending
    body = close - open
    wick = high - low

entries.title: Unterminated string literal
entries.message: This string literal opens with {quote} and the line ends before a matching {quote}.

placeholders.quote: the opening delimiter, a double or a single quote

entries.cause: A string literal may not span a line, so the scanner reports the opening quote rather than swallowing the rest of the file and complaining about the last line.
entries.fix: Close the string with a matching {quote} before the end of the line, and join text across lines with + and a continuation.

entries.title: Unknown escape sequence
entries.message: {sequence} is not an escape sequence.

placeholders.sequence: the backslash and the character that followed it

entries.cause: The escapes are a backslash followed by one of \ " ' n t r 0, and uXXXX with exactly four hexadecimal digits. Anything else is almost always a Windows path or a regular expression that was pasted without doubling its backslashes.
entries.fix: Double the backslash to write one literally, or use one of the escapes the language defines.

entries.title: Assignment used as a condition
entries.message: = assigns a value, and a condition needs a comparison.
entries.cause: Assignment is a statement and never an expression, so the classic typo cannot compile into a condition that is always true. There is no form of this language in which if x = 5 means anything.
entries.fix: Write == to compare, or move the assignment to its own line above the if.

entries.title: Semicolon
entries.message: ; is not part of the language.
entries.cause: A statement ends at the end of its line and a line holds at most one statement, so there is no separator to write.
entries.fix: Delete the ; and put the second statement on its own line.

entries.title: Chained comparison
entries.message: A comparison cannot be chained: {op1} is already applied before {op2}.

placeholders.op1: the first comparison operator on the line
placeholders.op2: the second comparison operator on the line

entries.cause: Two readings of a < b < c are plausible to a reader, the mathematical one and the C-family one, and a form with two plausible meanings has no place in a language that places orders. The grammar allows at most one comparison operator per expression.
entries.fix: Split it with and, naming the middle value twice: a < b and b < c.

entries.title: break or continue outside a loop
entries.message: {word} is only valid inside a for or a while body.

placeholders.word: break or continue, whichever was written

entries.cause: break leaves the innermost loop and continue starts its next iteration, so neither has a meaning where there is no loop to act on.
entries.fix: Move it inside the loop body, or write return to leave a function early.

example.before:
fn firstAbove(values, mark) =>
    if size(values) == 0
        break
    values[0]
example.after:
fn firstAbove(values, mark) =>
    if size(values) == 0
        return none
    values[0]

entries.title: Block header with no body
entries.message: {header} opens a block, and the next line is not indented more deeply.

placeholders.header: the keyword that opened the block, such as if, else, for, while, case or default

entries.cause: A header line introduces a block that consists of the following lines indented more deeply than the header. With nothing indented under it the header has no body, which is almost always a line that lost its indentation in a paste. Blank and comment-only lines carry no token, so they never count as a body: a header followed only by those, and then by a line at or left of the header, is still this error.
entries.fix: Indent the body under the header, or delete the header line if the body is genuinely empty.

entries.title: var with no initial value
entries.message: var {name} has no initial value.

placeholders.name: the name being declared

entries.cause: The declaration and the first assignment are one statement, so a persistent value always has something in it and no bar can read it before it exists.
entries.fix: Give it a starting value; var {name} = none is the empty start.

example.after:
var runningHigh = none
if isNone(runningHigh) or high > runningHigh
    runningHigh = high

entries.title: Bracket is never closed
entries.message: The {bracket} opened at line {line} is never closed.

placeholders.line: the line the bracket was opened on

entries.cause: An open ( or [ continues the statement onto the following lines, so a missing closer makes the scanner read the rest of the file as one statement. The error is reported at the opening bracket, which is where the mistake is.
entries.fix: Add the matching closer at the end of the argument list on line {line}.

entries.title: Mismatched closing bracket
entries.message: Found {found} where {expected} was expected, closing the {opener} opened at line {line}.

placeholders.found: the closing bracket that was written
placeholders.expected: the closing bracket the opener requires
placeholders.line: the line the bracket was opened on

entries.cause: Brackets nest, and a call closes with ) while an index or an array literal closes with ].
entries.fix: Change {found} to {expected}, which is what closes the {opener} opened at line {line}.

entries.title: Missing comma between arguments
entries.message: Two arguments run together; a comma is missing before {token}.

placeholders.token: the first token of the second argument

entries.cause: Arguments are separated by commas. Two expressions side by side inside a call are not a form the language has, so the missing comma is reported rather than guessed at.
entries.fix: Put a comma between the two arguments.

entries.title: Ternary with no second arm
entries.message: This ? has no matching :
entries.cause: The ternary always yields a value, so both arms are required. A ternary with one arm is usually a plot that wanted to draw nothing on some bars.
entries.fix: Give the ternary both arms, and use none for the arm that should draw nothing.

entries.title: else does not follow an if
entries.message: This else is indented {found} spaces and the nearest if is indented {expected}.

placeholders.found: the leading space count on the else line
placeholders.expected: the leading space count of the if it should pair with

entries.cause: An else pairs with the if at its own indentation. At any other indentation there is no if for it to belong to, and guessing which one was meant would make the block structure unreadable.
entries.fix: Line the else up with its if, at {expected} spaces.

entries.title: case or default in the wrong place
entries.message: {word} is only valid inside a switch, and default must be its last arm.

placeholders.word: case or default, whichever was written

entries.cause: The arms of a switch are its whole body. A default that is not last would leave the arms after it unreachable, which the language rejects rather than silently accepts.
entries.fix: Move the arm inside the switch block, and put default after every case.

example.before:
switch method
    default
        len = 14
    case "fast"
        len = 9
example.after:
switch method
    case "fast"
        len = 9
    default
        len = 14

entries.title: More than one statement on a line
entries.message: Unexpected {token} after the end of this statement.

placeholders.token: the first token that follows the complete statement

entries.cause: A line holds at most one statement, so anything after a statement ends is either a missing operator or a second statement that lost its newline. An assignment operator after an index or after a dotted name is not this error: the statement did not end there, and what is wrong is the target rather than anything following it. Those two are OS1024 and OS1025.
entries.fix: Put {token} and what follows it on its own line, or supply the operator that was meant to join them.

entries.title: Reserved word used as a name
entries.message: {word} is a reserved word and cannot be used as a name.

placeholders.word: the reserved word that was used as a name
placeholders.suggestion: a near name that is not reserved, derived from the word

entries.cause: The reserved words of language.md 3.4 include five that version 1 does not implement (import, map, matrix, type, as). They are reserved now so that implementing them later cannot break a script that used one as a name. A named argument label is not a name: it is matched against the callee's parameter list and is never looked up in any scope, so plot(v, "V", color = aqua) is correct and is not this error. The rule stops at the label. A parameter of a user function is an ordinary identifier, because the body refers to it, so fn f(color = red) is this error.
entries.fix: Rename it; {suggestion} keeps the meaning and is not reserved.

entries.title: Incomplete for header
entries.message: A for header needs = start to end or in array; found {token}.

placeholders.token: the token that appeared where to or in was expected

entries.cause: There are two loop forms and no third. A counted loop names a start and an end, and a loop over an array names the array.
entries.fix: Write for i = 0 to size(values) - 1 for a counted loop, or for v in values to visit elements.

entries.title: The version declaration is not first
entries.message: version must be the first line that is not blank and not a comment; line {line} came before it.

placeholders.line: the line of the first statement that preceded the version declaration

entries.cause: A host reads the version with a one-line scan so it can pick a front end before any parsing happens. A declaration further down the file would be read by the wrong front end, which defeats the purpose of having one.
entries.fix: Move the version line to the top of the file, above the study or strategy declaration.

entries.title: Expression expected
entries.message: An expression was expected after {token}.

placeholders.token: the operator or punctuation the statement ended on

entries.cause: An operator, a comma or an opening bracket at the end of a statement continues it onto the next line, so a statement that ends this way and is followed by nothing usable has lost its right-hand side.
entries.fix: Supply the missing operand, or delete the trailing {token}.

entries.title: A function declared inside a block
entries.message: fn {name} is declared inside a block, and a function is declared at the top level of the file.

placeholders.name: the function being declared

entries.cause: Functions may not be nested (language.md 11.1). A declaration under an if, a loop, a switch arm or another function's body sits in a scope that ends where the block ends, so the name would exist for part of a file and not the rest, and a reader would have to trace the block structure to know whether a call on the line in front of them was legal. The declaration is reported rather than dropped or lifted: dropping it leaves every call to it as OS2001 with no word about where the function went, and lifting it to the top level compiles a form the language does not have.
entries.fix: Move the whole declaration out to the top level of the file, and call {name} from inside the block.

entries.title: Assignment to an indexed element
entries.message: An assignment writes to a name, and this target is an index into {name}.

placeholders.name: the name that was indexed

entries.cause: The grammar of language.md 19 admits one assignment target, an identifier, and there is no indexed assignment anywhere in the language. The reason is that [] reads two different things (language.md 9.6): on an array it is an element, which section 14.1 writes with set(arr, i, v), and on a series it is a bar the engine has already computed, which nothing in a script may overwrite. One syntax covering both would read as though a past bar could be rewritten.
entries.fix: Change an array element with set({name}, i, v), or assign to a plain name: the past of a series is computed and never written.

entries.title: Assignment to a member
entries.message: An assignment writes to a name, and this target is the member {member} of {name}.

placeholders.name: the name written before the dot
placeholders.member: the name written after the dot

entries.cause: The grammar of language.md 19 admits one assignment target, an identifier. A dotted name reads a member of one of the namespaces on the closed list in language.md 15.2, and every member on that list is a per-bar fact, an instrument fact, a position fact or a function, each of them produced by the engine or by the host. There is nothing behind a dot that a script owns. Version 1 has no user-declared types that could add one either: type is a reserved word and is not implemented (language.md 18). A dotted name whose first half is not a namespace is the same answer for a simpler reason: it has no members at all.
entries.fix: Assign to a plain name. Version 1 has no member assignment: a dot reads a member, and the members a script can reach are facts and functions the library and the host supply.

entries.title: Block comment
entries.message: {marker} does not open or close a comment. A comment is written // and runs to the end of its line.

placeholders.marker: the two characters that were written, the opener or the closer

entries.cause: The language has line comments and no block form (language.md 3.2). The block form is left out on purpose: an unterminated one swallows the rest of a file and reports its error at the last line, which is the worst message a compiler can produce. Without the form there is nothing special about the two characters, so a divide and a multiply are what they are and the line parses as arithmetic with its operands missing. The diagnostics then land on the operators rather than on the comment that caused them, and a reader is told three things that are each true of a program they did not write. The marker is reported where it sits instead.
entries.fix: Write // instead, and give every line of a commented region its own //, which every editor does with one keystroke.

entries.title: Malformed colour literal
entries.message: {written} is not a colour: a colour literal is # and six or eight hexadecimal digits.

placeholders.written: the # and the run of characters written against it

entries.cause: A hexadecimal colour is # and six digits, two each for red, green and blue, or eight where the last two are the alpha byte (language.md 3.8). The three and four digit shorthands belong to other formats and this language does not have them, and a run of any other length, or one carrying a digit outside 0 to f, is a typing slip. It has a code of its own because every character in it is one the language accepts: the substitution row that gives OS1001 its sentence about # is written for a # outside a colour literal, and its advice, to delete the character or move the text into a string, would throw away a colour the writer had nearly right.
entries.fix: Give it six hexadecimal digits, or eight where the last two are the alpha byte. A named colour or rgb(r, g, b) says the same thing without the digits.

entries.title: A continuation line is not indented past its statement
entries.message: A continuation line must be indented more deeply than the line its statement began on; line {line} is indented {statement} and this line is indented {found}.

placeholders.found: the leading space count on this line
placeholders.statement: the leading space count of the line the statement began on
placeholders.line: the line the statement began on

entries.cause: A statement continues onto the next line when a bracket is still open, when the line ends with a binary operator, a comma, a ?, a : or an =, or when it ends with a backslash (language.md 3.11). A continuation is required to sit further right than the line the statement began on, so that a reader can tell a continued statement from a new one without scanning back up the file for a trailing operator. This is not the block rule of OS1003, and it has a code of its own for that reason: a continuation opens no block, so OS1003, whose message names the indentation every line of a block carries and whose fix offers to end that block, would state a fact about a block that is not there.
entries.fix: Indent this line further than the {statement} spaces on line {line}. Four more is the convention and the formatter's output.

entries.title: A name written against a number
entries.message: {written} is neither a number nor a name: the number literal ends at {number}, and a name cannot begin with a digit.

placeholders.written: the whole run, the number literal and the name characters against it
placeholders.number: the part of the run that is a number literal

entries.cause: A number literal is decimal, with an optional fractional part and an optional exponent, or 0x and hexadecimal digits. There is no octal form and no binary form, and an underscore belongs to a literal only where a digit follows it (language.md 3.5). A name cannot begin with a digit (language.md 3.3). A base prefix the language does not have, a unit written against a quantity, and a literal that ends in an underscore all produce this run. The whole run is reported rather than its first character, because every character in it is one the language accepts: naming the leading digit would name something legal, and deleting it, which is what OS1001 advises, leaves a valid name behind and a program that means something else.
entries.fix: Write the value in a form the language has: a decimal literal, or 0x and hexadecimal digits. There is no binary form and no octal form, and an underscore separates digit groups only where a digit follows it. Where a number and a name were meant as two things, put an operator between them.

entries.title: Name is not defined here
entries.message: {name} is not defined at this point in the file.

placeholders.name: the name that was read
placeholders.suggestion: the closest name that is in scope here, by edit distance

entries.cause: The file is the body of the per-bar loop and runs top to bottom, so a name must be assigned above the line that reads it. A name first assigned inside a block belongs to that block and is not visible outside it. A misspelling arrives here too.
entries.fix: Assign {name} above this line, move this line below its assignment, or correct the spelling to {suggestion}.

entries.title: The name already exists in an enclosing scope
entries.message: {name} is already declared at line {line}, so a second one cannot be declared here.

placeholders.name: the name being declared
placeholders.line: the line of the existing declaration, or the word built-in when it is a library name

entries.cause: There is no shadowing. An assignment to a name that exists in an enclosing scope updates that name, so declaring the same name inside is a request the language has no syntax for and is always a mistake. Built-in names such as close, ema, aqua and plot live in the global scope, so assigning to one lands here as well.
entries.fix: Rename this one, or drop the inner declaration and let the assignment update the {name} at line {line}.

example.before:
len = 20

fn smooth(src) =>
    len = 9
    sma(src, len)
example.after:
len = 20

fn smooth(src) =>
    inner = 9
    sma(src, inner)

entries.title: Types do not match
entries.message: {leftType} and {rightType} do not mix here.

placeholders.leftType: the type of the left operand or of the name's first assignment, or the words a per-bar value where the position takes a value of any type and a declaration handle was written
placeholders.rightType: the type of the right operand or of the value being assigned

entries.cause: There is no implicit conversion anywhere in the language: 0 is not false, an empty string is not false, and a number is not a string. A name's type is fixed by its first assignment, so assigning a different type later arrives here too. A first assignment of none fixes no type, because none is a member of every type; the type comes from the first assignment that gives a definite one, and this code names the second definite type rather than the first. Every silent coercion rule is a source of bugs that survive review, and a trading script that quietly treats a zero as a false is a bug nobody finds until it costs money. A declaration handle arrives here as well: plot(), plotCandles(), fill() and level() return the compile-time half of a declaration (language.md 5.4), so a handle in a position that requires a value has nothing to give, and the message names its type as plot, fill or level.
entries.fix: Convert explicitly: text(x) for a string, or text(x, decimals) to fix the decimals. Where no conversion applies, write the value in the type the line needs, or give the second value a name of its own. A plot, fill or level handle converts to nothing: leave it named at the top level, pass it to fill(), and use draw.line() or draw.box() where the script needs something it can keep.

entries.title: This value has no history
entries.message: {expr} has no history, so [] cannot read a past value of it.

placeholders.expr: the expression the history operator was applied to

entries.cause: History is retained for four kinds of value: a built-in series, a name assigned at the top level of the file, a call to a function declared to return a series, and a series parameter of a user function. Retaining it for every temporary inside every block would cost memory per bar and would not run fifty thousand bars in a browser tab. A name bound to a declaration handle is none of the four, although it sits at the top level: it is a compile-time binding with no per-bar value at all. A runtime object carries no history either, so [] on a line, a label, a box, a polyline or a table is this error as well (language.md 5.4).
entries.fix: If the value is a per-bar number computed inside a block or left as a temporary, assign it at the top level of the file and read the history of that top level name. If it is a declaration handle, a runtime object or a library fact that is not a series, no name gives it a history: assign what you want to look back at to a top level name of its own, and read that.

example.before:
if trending
    body = close - open
    plot(body[1], "Previous body", aqua)
example.after:
body = close - open
plot(trending ? body[1] : none, "Previous body", aqua)

entries.title: Recursive call
entries.message: {name} calls itself: {cycle}.

placeholders.name: the function at the start of the cycle
placeholders.cycle: the call chain, from the function back to itself

entries.cause: State slots for var and for stateful library calls are allocated statically, one per call site. Recursion would need a dynamic stack of them, whose cost would be paid on every bar of every script to support a form a per-bar language almost never needs.
entries.fix: Rewrite it as a loop, or split the work into two functions that do not call each other.

example.before:
fn total(n) =>
    if n <= 0
        return 0
    close[n] + total(n - 1)
example.after:
fn total(n) =>
    runningTotal = 0.0
    for i = 0 to n
        runningTotal += close[i]
    runningTotal

entries.title: Assignment to a loop variable
entries.message: {name} is this loop's variable and cannot be assigned inside the body.

placeholders.name: the loop variable

entries.cause: The loop controls its own variable, so a body that also writes to it produces a loop whose iteration count cannot be read from its header.
entries.fix: Use break to leave early, or keep a separate name for the value the body changes.

example.before:
for i = 0 to 9
    if close[i] > hi
        i = 9
example.after:
for i = 0 to 9
    if close[i] > hi
        break

entries.title: The file has no declaration
entries.message: A file needs one study() or strategy() declaration before any other statement.
entries.cause: The declaration supplies the title, the pane, the precision and the settings the host needs before the first bar runs. Without one there is nothing to put in a legend and nothing to name in a picker.
entries.fix: Add study("Name") as the first statement, or strategy("Name") if the file places orders.

example.after:
study("EMA", overlay = true)

fast = ema(close, 9)
plot(fast, "Fast", aqua)

entries.title: More than one declaration
entries.message: This file already declares {kind} at line {line}.

placeholders.kind: study or strategy, whichever came first
placeholders.line: the line of the first declaration

entries.cause: Two declarations would need a rule for whose overlay, precision and title win, and the answer to that question is always that there should have been one. A strategy accepts every study option, so a file that wants both is a strategy.
entries.fix: Delete this declaration and move the options you wanted onto the one at line {line}.

example.before:
study("EMA cross", overlay = true)
strategy("EMA cross")

entries.title: Unknown member of a namespace
entries.message: {namespace} has no member named {member}.

placeholders.member: the member name that does not exist
placeholders.suggestion: the closest member of that namespace, by edit distance

entries.cause: Namespaces hold a fixed set of names, published in the library manifest the editor completes from. A member that does not exist is a typo or a name from a different namespace.
entries.fix: Use one of {namespace}'s members; {suggestion} is the closest match to what was written.

entries.title: This name is not a function
entries.message: {name} is {type}, not a function, so it cannot be called.

placeholders.name: the name that was called
placeholders.suggestion: the library function whose name is closest, with its first argument filled in

entries.cause: A built-in series and a user value are read bare. An argument list after one of them is usually a library function that was remembered with the wrong name.
entries.fix: Remove the argument list to read the value, or call the function that was meant: {suggestion}.

entries.title: A condition must be a bool
entries.message: This condition is {type}; a condition must be bool or none.

placeholders.type: the type the condition expression produced
placeholders.name: the condition expression as written, or its name when it is one

entries.cause: There is no truthiness. A number is not a condition, a string is not a condition, and an absent value takes the false branch only after the condition has been written as a genuine test.
entries.fix: Write the test out: {name} > 0 for a count, isNone({name}) for absence, {name} != "" for a string.

entries.title: The two arms of the ternary have different types
entries.message: The arms of this ? : are {leftType} and {rightType}.

placeholders.leftType: the type of the arm before the colon
placeholders.rightType: the type of the arm after the colon

entries.cause: The ternary yields one value, so both arms must agree on its type. The one exception is none, which is a member of every type and is how an arm says there is nothing here.
entries.fix: Make both arms the same type with text() or toNumber(), or use none for the empty arm.

entries.title: An array literal mixes types
entries.message: This array holds {firstType} at index 0 and {otherType} at index {index}.

placeholders.firstType: the type of the first element
placeholders.otherType: the type of the element that disagrees
placeholders.index: the index of the element that disagrees

entries.cause: An array is homogeneous, which is what lets size, sum, avg and sort mean one thing. A mixed literal is usually two lists that belong side by side.
entries.fix: Make every element {firstType}, or keep two arrays and index them together.

entries.title: A function cannot be used as a value
entries.message: {name} is a function, and version 1 has no function values.

placeholders.name: the function name that was used bare

entries.cause: Functions are not values in version 1: they cannot be assigned, stored in an array or passed as an argument. The feature is reserved rather than absent, and language.md 18 names it.
entries.fix: Call {name} with its arguments and use the value it returns.

entries.title: The element type of this empty array is unknown
entries.message: An empty array literal needs its element type from an annotation or from a first use.
entries.cause: An array is homogeneous, so its element type has to be known before anything is pushed into it. An empty literal takes that type from an annotation when it has one, and otherwise from the first call in the file, in source order, that puts an element into it: push, unshift, insert or set. With neither an annotation nor such a call, nothing in the file says what the array holds and the language does not guess.
entries.fix: Annotate the declaration, var hits: array<number> = [], or put the first element in with push(), unshift(), insert() or set() and let the type be read from that call.

entries.title: Unknown type in an annotation
entries.message: {type} is not a type.

placeholders.type: the word that was written where a type was expected

entries.cause: The types are number, string, bool, color, none, array<T> and the five runtime object types line, label, box, polyline and table, with series in front where a per-bar value is meant. There is no integer type: a length, a bar count and a price are all number. The declaration handle types plot, fill and level are deliberately not in the grammar, so writing one in an annotation is this error as well: a handle can never be a var, a parameter, a return value or an array element, and there is nothing left for an annotation to describe.
entries.fix: Use number, string, bool, color, array<T>, or an object type (line, label, box, polyline, table), with series in front for a per-bar value.

example.before:
fn band(src: series number, len: int = 20) =>
    sma(src, len)
example.after:
fn band(src: series number, len: number = 20) =>
    sma(src, len)

entries.title: A function with this name is already declared
entries.message: {name} is already declared as a function at line {line}.

placeholders.name: the function name
placeholders.line: the line of the first declaration

entries.cause: A user function is not overloaded in version 1, so one name in a file is one function. Two declarations would make the call site's meaning depend on argument types, which is exactly the kind of resolution a reader cannot do in their head. The library's own overloads are a different thing: they are a fixed published set, round() and clear() among them, and a script cannot add to it.
entries.fix: Rename one of them, or give the one function a default argument that covers both uses.

example.before:
fn band(src) => sma(src, 20)
fn band(src, len) => sma(src, len)

entries.title: Duplicate parameter name
entries.message: {name} appears twice in this parameter list.

placeholders.name: the repeated parameter name

entries.cause: Two parameters with one name make every use of that name inside the body ambiguous, and a named argument at the call site could not say which one it meant.
entries.fix: Rename the second parameter, so every name in the list appears once.

entries.title: This type cannot be an array element
entries.message: array<{type}> is not a type: {type} cannot be an array element.

placeholders.type: the element type written inside the angle brackets

entries.cause: An array element is a number, a string, a bool, a color, or one of the runtime object types of language.md 5.4, and nothing else. A declaration handle is the compile-time half of a declaration and has no run-time value, so there would be nothing to store. A series is a per-bar history, and an array of them would be a second history the engine retained per element, as many as the script chose to push. An array of arrays is the matrix that language.md 14.2 reserves for a later version.
entries.fix: Use an element type an array holds: number, string, bool, color, line, label, box, polyline or table. A plot cannot be kept anywhere, so declare each plot at the top level and give it its own name.

example.before:
var edges: array<plot> = []
push(edges, plot(upper, "Upper", aqua))
example.after:
upperEdge = plot(upper, "Upper", aqua)
lowerEdge = plot(lower, "Lower", aqua)
fill(upperEdge, lowerEdge, color = fade(aqua, 88))

entries.title: Name is planned, not implemented
entries.message: {name} is planned and is not implemented in this version.

placeholders.name: the planned name that was called or read

entries.cause: The library names a few calls and facts it does not implement yet, so that the gap is visible rather than left for a reader to guess at (stdlib.md 1). The checker knows this name and knows it carries no behaviour, which is a different fact from a name it has never heard of: nothing about the spelling is wrong, no line above it would help, and the name starts working on a version that implements it.
entries.fix: Compute what {name} would give from names the library implements today, or take the line out until a version implements it. Do not reach for the nearest name that compiles: a neighbour computes something else, and a plot that quietly changes meaning is worse than one that refuses to compile.

example.after:
zScore = (close - sma(close, 20)) / stdev(close, 20)
doubled = exp(2 * zScore)
plot((doubled - 1) / (doubled + 1), "Squashed", aqua)

entries.title: Wrong number of arguments
entries.message: {name} takes {expected} arguments and {found} were given.

placeholders.name: the function being called
placeholders.expected: the number of parameters, or the range when some have defaults
placeholders.found: the number of arguments at this call site
placeholders.signature: the function's full signature, parameter names and defaults included

entries.cause: A call site is checked against the declared parameter list. Parameters with defaults may be left out, and every parameter without one must be supplied.
entries.fix: Pass the arguments the signature names: {signature}.

entries.title: Unknown named argument
entries.message: {name} has no argument called {argument}.

placeholders.name: the function being called
placeholders.argument: the named argument that does not exist
placeholders.names: every argument name the function accepts, in declaration order
placeholders.suggestion: the closest accepted name, by edit distance

entries.cause: Named arguments are matched against the parameter list by exact name. A name that is not on the list is a spelling that the call site and the function disagree about, and ignoring it would leave the argument silently unapplied.
entries.fix: Use one of {names}; {suggestion} is the closest to what was written.

entries.title: This option must be a constant
entries.message: {option} is read once, before the first bar, so it cannot depend on bar data.

placeholders.option: the option that was given a bar-dependent value

entries.cause: The declaration builds the legend, the axis and the settings dialog before bar 0 runs, so its options must be literals, arithmetic over literals, or an input() written as the whole of the value; an expression over an input is OS3025. A value that changes per bar has no single answer at the moment the dialog is built. The rule covers more than the declaration's own options: every argument that lands in a declaration fixed before bar 0 arrives here too, signal's at, shape and color, table's position, rows and cols, and a plot's style arguments among them. An input() counts as a constant for this purpose, because the engine resolves inputs at load and substitutes the resolved value before bar 0 runs.
entries.fix: Use a literal, or make it tunable with an input(): {option} = input(2, "{option}").

entries.title: Argument is not a valid whole number
entries.message: {name}'s {argument} must be a whole number {range}; {found} was given.

placeholders.name: the function being called
placeholders.range: the accepted range, such as 1 or more
placeholders.found: the literal value that was written

entries.cause: A lookback length, an index and a loop step are counts of bars or of elements. A fractional value is rejected rather than truncated, because a length of 14.5 is a bug in the script and rounding it hides the bug. A step of 0 is rejected because it is the one loop that cannot finish.
entries.fix: Pass a whole number inside {range}, and wrap a computed value in floor() or round().

entries.title: Positional argument after a named one
entries.message: A positional argument cannot follow a named one.
entries.cause: Once an argument is named, the position of the arguments after it no longer says which parameter they fill. The order is positional first, named afterwards, which keeps every call site readable without the signature in front of you.
entries.fix: Name this argument too, or move it in front of the first named argument.

entries.title: This call must be at the top level
entries.message: {name} defines part of the study's fixed shape and cannot appear inside {construct}.

placeholders.name: the call, one of plot, plotCandles, fill, level, table, leg.fixed or leg.relative
placeholders.construct: the enclosing construct, such as an if block, a loop or a function body

entries.cause: The set of plotted columns, bands, levels and grids is fixed before bar 0 so the chart can build a legend, an axis and a settings dialog. A call inside a branch would add a column on some bars and not others, and there would be nothing stable to name. table() is on the list for the same reason, the grid's size and corner being part of the study's fixed shape, although what it returns is a runtime object that cell() writes to per bar (language.md 5.4). A leg declaration is on the list for the same reason: the set of contracts a strategy trades is fixed before bar 0, and a leg that existed on some bars and not others would leave the run's record with nothing to key on. A drawing or an alert call inside a request expression is the same error for a related reason: that expression is evaluated on another instrument's bars, so there is no bar of this chart for it to draw on.
entries.fix: Move the call to the top level and hide it per bar by passing none: plot(cond ? value : none, ...). Inside a request expression, read the value first and draw with it afterwards. A leg is not hidden by passing none: declare it at the top level and decide per bar whether to send it an order.

entries.title: input() must be at the top level
entries.message: input() builds one row of the settings dialog, which is read once before the first bar.
entries.cause: The dialog exists before any bar runs, so every input has to be reachable without executing the script. An input inside a block would appear or vanish depending on the data, and a saved setting would have nothing to attach to.
entries.fix: Move the input() to the top level and use the name it assigns inside the block.

example.after:
len = input(20, "Length")
b = sma(close, len)
plot(useBand ? b : none, "Band", aqua)

entries.title: The value is not valid for this parameter
entries.message: {argument} accepts {values}; {found} is not one of them.

placeholders.argument: the parameter, option or setting key
placeholders.values: the accepted values or the accepted form, written out
placeholders.found: the value that was written or that the host supplied
placeholders.suggestion: the accepted value closest to what was written

entries.cause: Some parameters take a value out of a fixed set, or in a fixed written form, rather than free text, because each one selects a different rule in the engine or the report. Two cases arrive here: a name that is not in the set, and a structured string that does not parse, a session window for instance. An unknown name has no rule to select, and defaulting quietly would change what the script does without saying so. The same failure in a setting the host supplied is OS6019, because there the value came from outside the source.
entries.fix: Use one of {values}; {suggestion} is the closest to what was written.

entries.title: This option needs another option to be set
entries.message: {option} = {value} requires {required}.

placeholders.value: the value it was set to
placeholders.required: the option and value it depends on

entries.cause: A few options only mean something in combination. An alert that fires on every execution of a bar only has executions to fire on in a file that acts on unconfirmed bars. Accepting the option on its own would leave it doing nothing, silently, which is the worst of the three possible behaviours.
entries.fix: Set {required} in the declaration, or choose a value of {option} that stands on its own.

example.before:
study("Ticks")

if close > open
    alert("Up", id = "up", frequency = "everyUpdate")
example.after:
study("Ticks", onUnconfirmed = true)

if close > open
    alert("Up", id = "up", frequency = "everyUpdate")

entries.title: Two arguments that cannot both be given
entries.message: {first} and {second} set the same thing two ways.

placeholders.first: the first of the two arguments
placeholders.second: the second of the two arguments

entries.cause: Two arguments that set one thing have to be reconciled, and every rule for reconciling them surprises somebody, so the call is refused and the script says which it meant. There are three pairs. An exit level can be written as an absolute price or as a distance from the entry, and the candidate rules (the nearer one, the later one, the absolute one) each surprise someone. A band takes color for both of its sides, or colorUp and colorDown for the leading and the lagging side, and color together with either of those leaves no answer for which side wins. The third is a relative leg described as a future and given a right or a strike offset, which are fields of an option.
entries.fix: Keep one of the two: an absolute price or a distance from the entry, one colour for the whole band or a colour for each side, and on a leg described as a future neither right nor strikeOffset.

entries.title: Argument has the wrong type
entries.message: {name}'s {argument} is {expected}; {found} was given.

placeholders.name: the function being called
placeholders.found: the type of the expression at the call site

entries.cause: Arguments are checked against the declared parameter types, with broadcast as the only widening: a plain value may be passed where a series is expected, and it is read as that same value on every bar. Nothing else converts on its own. A declaration handle passed to an argument that does not take one arrives here too; where that argument wanted a runtime object the case has its own code, OS3019, and fill's two plot arguments have OS3020.
entries.fix: Convert the value with text(), toNumber() or toBool(), or pass an expression of type {expected}.

entries.title: A required argument is missing
entries.message: {name} requires {argument}, which has no default.

placeholders.name: the function being called
placeholders.argument: the parameter that was left out
placeholders.example: a filled-in call showing the argument in place

entries.cause: A parameter without a default has no value the engine could invent. The title of a study and the source of an indicator are the common cases, and an order's leg argument in a file that declares more than one leg is a third: with several contracts to choose from there is none the engine could pick.
entries.fix: Pass {argument} at the call site, as the example shows: {example}.

entries.title: Argument given twice
entries.message: {argument} is given twice at this call site.

placeholders.argument: the parameter that received two values

entries.cause: A named argument may not repeat one already filled by position, and may not appear twice. Either would leave the reader guessing which value wins.
entries.fix: Delete one of the two, keeping the value that was meant.

entries.title: limits() is in the wrong place
entries.message: limits() appears at most once, immediately after the declaration; this one is at line {line}.

placeholders.line: the line the limits() call was found on

entries.cause: The budgets apply to the whole run and are read before the first bar. One fixed position means a reader can see a script's budgets without searching the file, and two calls would need a rule for which one wins.
entries.fix: Move the limits() line directly under study(...) or strategy(...), and merge two calls into one.

entries.title: limits() takes literal numbers
entries.message: limits() is read before the first bar, so {option} must be a literal number.

placeholders.option: the limits option that was given a computed value

entries.cause: The engine allocates against these budgets before it runs anything, so there is no bar on which a computed budget could be evaluated. An input() is not accepted here either, because a budget that a settings dialog can change is a budget a reader cannot see.
entries.fix: Write the number: limits(loops = 50_000_000).

entries.title: range must be a low and a high
entries.message: range is [{low}, {high}]; it takes two numbers and the first must be below the second.
entries.cause: The range option fixes the study pane's scale, so it is exactly two numbers in axis order. A reversed or single-element range has no scale to build.
entries.fix: Write two numbers, lowest first: range = [0, 100].

entries.title: Two of these share a name
entries.message: {kind} names must be unique in a file; {name} is also used at line {line}.

placeholders.kind: the thing being named: plot, plotCandles, level, input, table, alert or leg
placeholders.name: the repeated name, quoted
placeholders.line: the line of the first use of that name

entries.cause: The legend row, the settings dialog and the saved layout all key a column by its name, and an alert message names it. Two columns with one name would overwrite each other's saved settings. fill is not on the list: a band has no name of its own and is identified by the two plots it is drawn between. A leg's name is what every later call keys on, so two legs with one name leave every leg call with no answer. An alert is named by its id, written or derived from the line, and a subscription is kept under that name, so two alerts sharing one leave the user subscribed to whichever of the two the host kept.
entries.fix: Rename one of them so each name appears once.

example.after:
plot(fast, "EMA fast", aqua)
plot(slow, "EMA slow", orange)

entries.title: The default is not in the options list
entries.message: This input's default {default} is not one of options {values}.
entries.cause: An input with options is a dropdown, and its default is the row that is selected when the dialog opens. A default outside the list leaves the dialog with nothing selected and the script with a value the user cannot reproduce.
entries.fix: Add {default} to options, or make the default one of the listed values.

entries.title: A declaration handle in an object argument
entries.message: {name}'s {argument} is {expected}; {found} is a declaration handle, which has no value at run time.

placeholders.name: the function being called
placeholders.expected: the object type the parameter takes
placeholders.found: the handle type at the call site: plot, fill or level

entries.cause: plot(), plotCandles(), fill() and level() return a declaration handle: the compile-time half of a declaration, an entry in the program's outputs, with no run-time representation at all. The draw setters, cell() and clear() take a runtime object, which is a value the script made on a bar and can keep, move and delete. The two kinds are separated in the type system for exactly this reason, and fill() is the one call in version 1 that takes a handle.
entries.fix: Pass an object the script created with draw.line(), draw.box() or draw.label(), and change a plot's own appearance through the arguments of the plot call instead.

example.before:
upper = plot(basis + dev, "Upper", aqua)
draw.setColor(upper, red)
example.after: plot(basis + dev, "Upper", color = close > basis ? lime : red)

entries.title: fill needs two declared plots
entries.message: fill's {argument} is {found}; it takes a plot declared by plot() or plotCandles().

placeholders.argument: the parameter that was given the wrong thing, plotA or plotB
placeholders.found: the type of the expression at the call site

entries.cause: A band is one entry of the chart contract's shaded bands, and that entry holds the two plot keys the band is drawn between (compiled-program.md 2.8). A bare expression has no key, because no column was ever declared for it, so there is nothing in the contract for it to compile into. Naming the two edges is what makes a band readable as well: it is drawn between two columns the chart already shows, rather than instead of them.
entries.fix: Plot both edges at the top level, name each one, and pass the two names to fill().

example.before: fill(basis + dev, basis - dev, color = fade(aqua, 88))
example.after:
upper = plot(basis + dev, "Upper", aqua)
lower = plot(basis - dev, "Lower", aqua)
fill(upper, lower, color = fade(aqua, 88))

entries.title: An input written in place has no title
entries.message: An input() assigned to no name is named by its title, and this one has no title written as a string literal.
entries.cause: A host stores one value per input key, and the key is the name the input was assigned to (host-interface.md 8.1). An input written where a value belongs is assigned to no name, so its title is its key as well as its dialog label. The title is read from the line as a string literal rather than folded, because a key and a label are both fixed before anything is computed and because the row a reader sees should be named on the line that declares it. With neither a name nor such a title there is nothing to label the row with and nothing to store a user's value under, and a key made from the input's position instead would move the moment another input was written above it, taking a user's stored value onto a different row.
entries.fix: Give it a title written as a string literal: input(2, "Precision").

entries.title: Two inputs share a settings key
entries.message: This input is keyed by its title {name}, which is already the name of the input at line {line}.

placeholders.name: the title of the input written in place, quoted
placeholders.line: the line of the input that already carries that key

entries.cause: A host stores one value per key (host-interface.md 8.1). An input assigned to a name is keyed by that name, and one written in place is keyed by its title, so a title that spells another input's name puts two rows on one key. One user value would then serve two rows and nothing anywhere decides which of them gets it. Two inputs carrying one title are OS3017 for the same reason.
entries.fix: Give this one a title of its own, or rename the input at line {line}.

example.before:
width = input(2, "Width")
plot(close + width * input(3, "width"), "Band", aqua)
example.after:
width = input(2, "Width")
plot(close + width * input(3, "Multiplier"), "Band", aqua)

entries.title: An order names a leg this file does not declare
entries.message: {name} was given a {argument}, and this file declares none.

placeholders.name: the order function that was called
placeholders.argument: the parameter that names the declaration, which is leg

entries.cause: Every order function names the leg it acts on, and a leg is a contract declared before the run (stdlib.md 17.1, 17.6). A file that declares no leg has exactly one, the instrument its chart is showing, and every order acts on it with no leg named. So in a file with no leg declaration there is no name a leg argument could carry, and one written there names nothing. Ignored, it is silent in the most expensive way an order can be: a script that entered under one name and closed another flattened the only leg there is and was told nothing, and a name the script computed was dropped just as quietly. It is refused whatever the argument holds, rather than held against a list of accepted values the way OS3008 holds every other fixed set, because here the list is empty and the value is not what is wrong.
entries.fix: Leave {argument} out. A file that declares no leg has exactly one, and every order acts on it.

example.before:
if pos.isFlat
    buy(qty = 1, leg = "hedge")
else
    close()

entries.title: An input written in place has an empty title
entries.message: An input() assigned to no name is named by its title, and this one's title is empty.
entries.cause: The title of an input written where a value belongs is its settings key as well as its dialog label (host-interface.md 8.1), and the empty string is neither. There is nothing to store a user's value under and nothing to label the row with, and a second input written the same way would land on the same empty key and take the same stored value. This is the case OS3021 refuses, reached by a different edit, and it carries its own code because OS3021 tells a reader to give the input a title written as a string literal and this reader has written one. A message and a fix that are both already true of the program in front of somebody send them to change nothing. What is wrong here is not that the title was left out: it is that the title says nothing, and the fix is to give it something to say. An input assigned to a name is not this. It has a key already, and an empty title there is read as no title and labelled with the name, which language.md 13.4 states.
entries.fix: Give the title something to say: input(2, "Precision").

entries.title: A setting is part of a larger expression here
entries.message: {option} is fixed before the first bar and holds an input() only as the whole of its value, so it cannot hold an expression over one.

placeholders.option: the option or field whose value reads a setting as part of something larger

entries.cause: A field fixed before bar 0 is written into the compiled program as one of two things: the value itself, which the compiler folds, or a reference to one input, which the engine resolves once at load (compiled-program.md 2.3). An expression over a setting is neither. The compiler cannot fold it, because the setting's value is not known until the host resolves the settings, and the program has no form for an expression evaluated at load, because that would be a second evaluator every engine has to agree on before the first bar. An input's own default, bounds and step are the same kind of field and are held tighter still: they are what the settings dialog shows before anybody has chosen, so none of them may read another setting at all.
entries.fix: Declare the setting as the value itself, with an input() written as the whole of {option}, or write the value out as a literal.

example.before:
w = input(1, "Width")
plot(close, "Close", aqua, width = w + 1)
example.after:
w = input(2, "Width")
plot(close, "Close", aqua, width = w)

entries.title: This option cannot be a setting
entries.message: {option} is written into the compiled program as a plain value, so a setting cannot choose it in this format version.

placeholders.option: the option that was written from an input()

entries.cause: An option fixed before bar 0 carries either its value or a reference to one input, resolved at load (compiled-program.md 2.3), and almost every option takes both. A plot's style takes only the value: its field in the compiled format is a plain string. So an input() written into it could only be folded to its default, the settings row it declares would move nothing, and a select offering values the option does not accept would pass, because the set check reads a value written out and a setting is not one. Widening the field changes the compiled format that every other engine is written against, so it is refused here rather than half carried.
entries.fix: Write the option out as a string literal and drop the input(): style = "step", for instance, is one of the values OS3008 names.

example.before:
st = input("line", "Style", options = ["line", "step", "area"])
plot(close, "Close", aqua, style = st)

entries.title: History index is not usable
entries.message: [{index}] is not a whole number of bars at or above zero.

placeholders.index: the value the index expression produced on this bar

entries.cause: A history index counts bars back, so it is a whole number and it is never negative: reading the future is not available at any price. A negative literal is caught at compile time as OS3004; this is the computed case.
entries.fix: Wrap the index in floor() or round(), and clamp a computed index with max(0, n).

entries.title: History index is deeper than the retained depth
entries.message: [{index}] reaches past the retained depth of {depth} bars.

placeholders.depth: the depth the host or the script set
placeholders.suggested: an adequate depth for this script, being the deepest index it uses

entries.cause: The value existed and the engine discarded it, which is a different situation from a value that never existed. Conflating the two would hide a real bug behind a plausible gap, so this is an error while a read past the start of history is simply absent.
entries.fix: Raise the depth in one place: limits(history = {suggested}).

entries.title: A whole number was required here
entries.message: {name}'s {argument} was {found} on this bar; a whole number was required.

placeholders.name: the function being called
placeholders.found: the value that reached the call

entries.cause: An index, a digit count and a repeat count are whole numbers. Where the value is a literal the checker catches it as OS3004; where it is computed it arrives here, on the bar that produced it.
entries.fix: Round the value before passing it: floor() towards zero, round() to nearest.

entries.title: Array index out of range
entries.message: Index {index} is outside {name}, which holds {size} elements.

placeholders.name: the array's name
placeholders.size: the array's element count on this bar

entries.cause: An array has an extent the script chose, so an index outside it is a mistake rather than a missing measurement. This is deliberately the opposite of the history operator, where reading past the start of history is absence.
entries.fix: Guard the read with size({name}), and index from size({name}) - 1 for the last element.

entries.title: The drawing object no longer exists
entries.message: This {kind} was deleted on bar {bar} and cannot be changed.

placeholders.kind: the object kind: line, label, box or polyline
placeholders.bar: the bar index the object was deleted on

entries.cause: An object lives from the bar that created it until the bar that deletes it, and nothing else ends its life: dropping the last name that refers to one leaves it on the chart, because there is no collection of unreachable objects. This error is the other side of that rule. A name kept in a var outlives the object it was given, so a setter reaching a deleted object is a script that has lost track of its own state and will go on doing so. A table never arrives here, because a table is never deleted: clear(t) empties it and the grid lives as long as the study. OS8019 warns about the shape that leads here, at compile time.
entries.fix: Assign none to the name on the same path as the delete, and test isNone() on it before changing the object.

example.before:
var top = none
if isNone(top)
    top = draw.line(time, low, time, high)
if close < open
    draw.delete(top)
draw.setTo(top, time, high)
example.after:
var top = none
if isNone(top)
    top = draw.line(time, low, time, high)
if close < open
    draw.delete(top)
    top = none
if not isNone(top)
    draw.setTo(top, time, high)

entries.title: The array is empty
entries.message: {name} cannot take an element from an empty array.

placeholders.name: the call, one of pop, shift, min, max or avg

entries.cause: Removing or summarising an element of an empty array has no answer. Returning absence would let a script drain an array without noticing, which is the bug this catches.
entries.fix: Test size(arr) > 0 before the call.
entries.deferred: Nothing raises this yet. Taking an element from an empty array raises the broader OS4004, and summarising one returns absence, which is the silent drain this entry exists to refuse. Raised when the array library tells the empty case apart from an index outside a filled array, language.md 14.1.

entries.title: Slice range is invalid
entries.message: slice({from}, {to}) is not a range inside an array of {size} elements.

placeholders.size: the array's element count on this bar

entries.cause: A slice takes from inclusive and to exclusive, so a valid range satisfies 0 <= from <= to <= size. A reversed range is not read backwards, because a slice that silently reverses is a slice nobody can read.
entries.fix: Clamp the bounds: from = max(0, from) and to = min(size(arr), to), with from at or below to.
entries.deferred: Nothing raises this yet. slice takes whatever range it is given and returns a shortened or empty array, so a reversed or out of range pair produces a plausible answer instead of a refusal. Raised when the array library checks the range against the array, language.md 14.1.

entries.title: Table cell is outside the table
entries.message: Cell ({row}, {column}) is outside a table of {rows} rows and {columns} columns.

placeholders.row: the row index that was written to
placeholders.column: the column index that was written to

entries.cause: A table's shape is declared once, with the study's fixed surface, so a write outside it has no cell to land in. Growing the table on demand would change the layout between bars and would make a saved layout meaningless.
entries.fix: Declare the table with the shape the script writes: table("Summary", {rows}, {columns}).

entries.title: Colour channel is out of range
entries.message: {name}'s {argument} is {found}; channels run 0 to 255 and alpha runs 0 to 1.

placeholders.name: the colour function: rgb, rgba or fade
placeholders.argument: the channel that was out of range
placeholders.found: the value that reached the call

entries.cause: A colour channel outside its range has no rendering, and clamping silently would make a study whose colours are a computation look right at the edges and wrong in between.
entries.fix: Clamp the value where it is computed: rgb(min(255, max(0, r)), g, b).
entries.deferred: Nothing raises this yet. The colour calls build a colour from whatever channels they are given, so a channel outside its range reaches the chart rather than stopping the bar. Raised when the colour library checks each channel, language.md 3.8.

entries.title: Calendar field is out of range
entries.message: {field} is {found}; it runs {range}.

placeholders.field: the calendar field: year, month, day, hour, minute or second
placeholders.found: the value that reached the call
placeholders.range: the accepted range for that field

entries.cause: A date is built from fields that each have a range, and a month of 13 is a script bug rather than a date. Rolling over into the next year would turn an off-by-one into a silently wrong timestamp, which in a session test is a whole day of wrong signals.
entries.fix: Pass a value inside {range}, carrying the overflow into the field above it as the example does.
entries.deferred: Nothing raises this yet. Building a date returns absence only when a field is not a whole number, so a month past the end of the year rolls into the next one and becomes a timestamp the script never meant. Raised when the calendar library checks each field against its range, language.md 15.2.

entries.title: String position is outside the string
entries.message: Position {index} is outside a string of {length} characters.
entries.cause: A string position addresses an existing character, counted in Unicode code points. Returning an empty string instead would let a parsing loop run off the end and produce a plausible empty result.
entries.fix: Guard with str.length(s), or clamp the position with min() before the call.
entries.deferred: Nothing raises this yet. Taking part of a string slices the code points it holds, so a position outside the string returns a shorter string or an empty one, which is the plausible empty result this entry refuses. Raised when the string library checks the position against the string, language.md 15.2.

entries.title: That value is not one of the accepted names
entries.message: {argument} accepts {values}; {found} was computed on this bar.

placeholders.values: every accepted value, quoted and comma separated
placeholders.found: the value that reached the call

entries.cause: The compile-time form of this is OS3008. Where the value is computed, the check happens on the bar that produced it, because a name that selects an engine rule cannot be guessed at and cannot be defaulted without changing what the script does.
entries.fix: Produce the value from an input() with an options list, so only accepted names can reach the call.
entries.deferred: Nothing raises this yet. A computed name outside the accepted set produces absence on every bar rather than stopping, and only a name written as a literal is refused, at compile time, with OS3008. Raised when the engine checks a computed name on the bar that produced it, language.md 14.1.

entries.title: A loop bound is absent
entries.message: This loop's {bound} is absent on this bar.

placeholders.bound: the bound that was absent: start, limit or step

entries.cause: A counted loop needs three numbers before it can begin. Absence propagates through arithmetic and comparison, but a loop cannot propagate it: it either runs or it does not. Treating an absent bound as zero iterations would skip work the script asked for and leave a plot that looks computed, so the bar stops instead.
entries.fix: Give the bound a value with orElse(), or guard the loop with isNone() so a warmup bar skips it deliberately.

example.before:
for i = 0 to lookback
    total += close[i]

entries.title: Loop budget exhausted
entries.message: This bar used its {budget} loop iterations, and the loop at line {line} was still running.

placeholders.budget: the per-bar iteration budget in force
placeholders.line: the line of the loop that was running when the budget ran out
placeholders.suggested: a budget that would have completed this bar, rounded up

entries.cause: Every iteration of every loop counts against one per-bar budget, so a script with one nested loop is treated like a script with ten sequential ones, and the budget resets each bar so a long dataset is not itself a reason to fail. The bar stops rather than breaking out of the loop, because a loop that ran two million times and then stopped produces a plausible wrong number, which is worse than no number.
entries.fix: Fix the exit condition, or raise the budget in one line: limits(loops = {suggested}).

example.after:
while i < 500 and close[i] > close[i + 1]
    total += close[i]
    i += 1

entries.title: The array is too large
entries.message: An array holds at most {max} elements; {name} reached {size}.

placeholders.name: the array's name

entries.cause: The ceiling exists so that one script cannot exhaust a browser tab's memory and take the chart with it. It is not raised by limits() in version 1, because an array that large is almost always a window that is never trimmed.
entries.fix: Drop the oldest element as you append: if size(arr) > 500, shift(arr).

example.after:
var window = [0.0]
push(window, close)
if size(window) > 500
    shift(window)

entries.unexercised: The ceiling is the engine's own and it is a large one, so an example that reached it would be a run long enough to fill it rather than a script anybody would read. The before block shows the window that is never trimmed, which is the shape that gets there, and not the bar it stops on.

entries.title: The host refused this limits() value
entries.message: This host allows {option} up to {max}; the file asks for {found}.

placeholders.found: the value the file asked for

entries.cause: A host that will not run a budget says so instead of quietly capping it, because a script that silently ran under a smaller budget would produce numbers its author never asked for and could not reproduce.
entries.fix: Lower {option} to {max} or below, or run the file on a host that allows more.

entries.title: The program needs more state regions than the engine allows
entries.message: This program needs {found} state regions and the engine allows {max}; {first} calls {second} on several paths.

placeholders.found: the number of state regions the compiler would allocate
placeholders.first: the outer function in the nesting that caused it
placeholders.second: the function it calls more than once

entries.cause: State is allocated per call path, which is what lets one function body serve many independent pieces of state. The number of paths grows multiplicatively when several functions each call the next more than once. The compiler reports it rather than emitting a program no engine will load.
entries.fix: Call the inner function once at the top level, give its result a name, and pass that name down.

entries.title: Nesting is too deep
entries.message: {construct} is nested {found} deep and the ceiling is {max}.

placeholders.construct: the construct that nested too deeply: an expression, a block or a call
placeholders.found: the nesting depth reached

entries.cause: The ceiling keeps the parser, the checker and the engine inside a bounded stack, so no input can stop a tab. It applies to source nesting at compile time and to call depth at run time, and it is far above anything a person writes by hand: generated source is the usual way to reach it.
entries.fix: Flatten it: give the inner expression a name at the top level and use the name.
entries.unexercised: The ceiling is far above anything written by hand, which is the whole point of it: generated source is how a file reaches it. The before block shows the shape at four levels, where a reader can see it, and nothing that short can raise the code.

entries.title: Too many outstanding data requests
entries.message: This file makes {found} data requests and the host allows {max}.

placeholders.found: the number of distinct requests in the file
placeholders.max: the host's ceiling on concurrent requests

entries.cause: Each higher timeframe or other-instrument read is a separate series the host fetches and keeps in step with the chart. The ceiling is the host's, and it is reported rather than silently dropping the requests past it, because a dropped request is a plot that quietly turns absent.
entries.fix: Keep one request per symbol and timeframe, reuse the name it assigns, and delete the requests whose results are unused.

example.before:
dayHigh = req.timeframe("1D", high)
prevHigh = req.timeframe("1D", high)[1]
weekHigh = req.timeframe("1W", high)
example.after:
dayHigh = req.timeframe("1D", high)
prevHigh = dayHigh[1]
weekHigh = req.timeframe("1W", high)

entries.title: The bar took too long
entries.message: Bar {bar} ran for {ms} ms and the host allows {max} ms.

placeholders.bar: the bar index that exceeded the budget

entries.cause: A server running many strategies gives each bar a wall-clock budget, so one script cannot starve the rest. Work that does not change from bar to bar is the usual cause: recomputing over the whole history on every bar turns a linear study into a quadratic one.
entries.fix: Keep a running value in a var and update it per bar instead of recomputing over the whole history.

example.before:
total = 0.0
for i = 0 to bar.index
    total += close[i]

entries.title: The string is too long
entries.message: A string holds at most {max} characters; this one reached {found}.

placeholders.found: the length that was reached

entries.cause: The ceiling catches the one shape that grows without bound by accident: text appended to a persistent string on every bar, which is a log that nothing ever trims.
entries.fix: Keep the pieces in an array, trim it to the rows you display, and join only those.

example.after:
var logLines: array<string> = []
push(logLines, text(close))
if size(logLines) > 50
    shift(logLines)

entries.unexercised: The ceiling is the engine's own and a bar appends a few characters, so reaching it takes a run of thousands of bars rather than an example. The before block shows the log that is never trimmed, which is the shape that gets there.

entries.title: The program is too large
entries.message: This file compiles to {found} instructions and the ceiling is {max}.

placeholders.found: the instruction count the compiler produced

entries.cause: The compiled program is held in memory per chart and per running strategy, so it has a size the host is willing to hold. A file at this size is nearly always repeated blocks that a function would collapse.
entries.fix: Move the repeated block into a fn and call it, and delete branches the script no longer uses.

example.before:
a1 = sma(close, 10)
a2 = sma(close, 20)
a3 = sma(close, 30)
example.after:
fn avgOf(len) => sma(close, len)
a1 = avgOf(10)
a2 = avgOf(20)
a3 = avgOf(30)

entries.title: Too many drawing objects
entries.message: A script holds at most {max} drawing objects; this one would be number {found}.

placeholders.max: the number of drawing objects the host will hold at once
placeholders.found: the count the object being created would have reached

entries.cause: An object lives until the script deletes it, so a script that creates one on every bar and deletes none grows for as long as the chart is open, and nothing can reclaim it: an undeleted object is held by the chart whether or not the script still names it. The ceiling is the host's, and reaching it stops the bar and names the number. The oldest object is never dropped to make room, because a study that is correct on the right of the chart and quietly wrong on the left is worse than one that stops.
entries.fix: Delete each object when it stops being wanted, and bound the set: keep the objects in an array, and when it is longer than you want, delete the oldest object and remove the element.

example.before:
var zones: array<box> = []
push(zones, draw.box(time, low, time, high))
example.after:
var zones: array<box> = []
push(zones, draw.box(time, low, time, high))
if size(zones) > 50
    draw.delete(element(zones, 0))
    shift(zones)

entries.unexercised: The ceiling is the host's and a bar creates one object, so reaching it takes a run of thousands of bars rather than an example. The before block shows the script that creates on every bar and deletes on none, which is the shape that gets there.

entries.title: Unknown timeframe
entries.message: {value} is not a timeframe.

placeholders.value: the string that was passed as a timeframe

entries.cause: A timeframe is a count and a unit, written as a string: m for minutes, h for hours, D for days, W for weeks and M for months. The unit letters are case sensitive, so "1M" is one month and "1m" is one minute. A bare number is read as minutes, because that is the form an interval input supplies, so "60" and "1h" are the same timeframe.
entries.fix: Write a count and a unit, or a bare number of minutes: "5m", "1h", "1D", "1W", "60".

entries.title: The requested timeframe is lower than the chart's
entries.message: The chart is {chart} and the request asks for {requested}.
entries.cause: Folding a lower timeframe into a higher bar needs data from inside the bar, which the chart was not given. Inventing it is the definition of a repainting study, so the request is refused rather than approximated.
entries.fix: Request {chart} or higher, or change the chart's interval to the lower one and fold upwards instead.
